title: Conclusions & Generalizations — Skill Check
description: Draw a supported conclusion, preserve scope, and transfer a principle only when conditions fit.
subject: rla
passage:
A youth gardening program wanted to reduce afternoon heat inside four small tool shelters. Volunteers covered each shelter with a different roof material but kept the buildings the same size and measured indoor temperature at the same times for ten clear afternoons.

Shelter A kept its original dark metal roof and was usually the hottest. Shelter B received a white coating and averaged several degrees cooler. Shelter C was covered with a raised fabric layer that created an air gap; it performed well on breezy afternoons but less consistently when the air was still. Shelter D received a reflective panel above a thin foam layer and had the lowest average afternoon temperature. However, that system was heavier and required stronger roof supports.

The differences among shelters were larger on the hottest sunny days and smaller when afternoon clouds moved in. Volunteers concluded that roof color, reflectivity, insulation, and airflow can all affect heat gain, but they did not name one material as best for every building. A lightweight shelter may not safely support the heaviest system, while a site with steady airflow may benefit more from a raised fabric design. The team plans to repeat the trial during the rainy season before choosing materials for the program’s larger storage buildings.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the ten-afternoon trial?
questions.explanation: This choice best matches the passage: Several roof properties can reduce heat, but their benefits and tradeoffs differ.
questions.rule: Keep the answer within the passage’s actual scope.

options.text: Any roof change will produce exactly the same cooling effect.
Dark metal roofs are unsafe in every climate.
options.whyWrong: The trial measured heat in four shelters and does not establish universal safety.

options.text: Several roof properties can reduce heat, but their benefits and tradeoffs differ.
The heaviest roof system should be installed on every shelter.
options.whyWrong: The passage notes structural limits for heavier systems.

questions.prompt: Which generalization best fits the evidence?
questions.explanation: This choice best matches the passage: A cooling material should be chosen with both thermal performance and site/building constraints in mind.
questions.rule: Keep the answer within the passage’s actual scope.

options.text: A cooling material should be chosen with both thermal performance and site/building constraints in mind.
The material with the lowest temperature in one trial is automatically best everywhere.
options.whyWrong: The authors reject a universal choice.

options.text: Airflow never affects roof performance.
options.whyWrong: The fabric system changed with wind conditions.

options.text: Cloudy weather increases differences among roof materials.
options.whyWrong: The differences became smaller with clouds.

questions.prompt: What broader conclusion can be drawn from the change in temperature differences on cloudy afternoons?
questions.explanation: This choice best matches the passage: The advantage of a cooling roof can depend partly on weather conditions.
questions.rule: Keep the answer within the passage’s actual scope.

options.text: The measuring equipment stopped working in clouds.
All roofs become equally hot whenever clouds appear.
options.whyWrong: The passage says differences become smaller, not necessarily zero.

options.text: Clouds make structural support unimportant.
options.whyWrong: Structural capacity is a separate consideration.

options.text: The advantage of a cooling roof can depend partly on weather conditions.

questions.prompt: A new shelter has a weak roof frame but sits in a reliably breezy location. Which transfer is most reasonable from the trial?
questions.explanation: This choice best matches the passage: Consider the raised fabric system because its lighter approach performed well with airflow.
questions.rule: Keep the answer within the passage’s actual scope.

options.text: Use the heavy reflective-and-foam system because it had the lowest average temperature.
options.whyWrong: The weak frame makes the heavy system a poor automatic transfer.

options.text: Consider the raised fabric system because its lighter approach performed well with airflow.
Keep dark metal because every modification failed in wind.
options.whyWrong: The passage reports the opposite for the fabric layer.

options.text: Choose based only on rainy-season performance, which the trial already measured.
options.whyWrong: Rainy-season testing has not occurred yet.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion would overgeneralize the study?

options.text: Reflective materials can reduce heat gain under some conditions.

options.text: Reflective panels with foam are the best roof choice for every building in every season.
